bullets.text: We will cover databases, relational tables, keys, normalization, structured query language, and transactions.
Database: Organized collection of related data.
For example, a university may store student details, course information, faculty records, and examination results in a database.
Database management system: Software used to create, read, update, and manage data.
The database contains the data, the management system provides tools and rules for working with it.
Table: Contains rows and columns.
Each row represents one record, and each column represents an attribute.
A student table might contain student ID, name, email address, and department ID.
The table schema describes its columns and the kinds of values they can store.
Keys help identify records and connect tables.
A primary key uniquely identifies each row.
Foreign key: Key in another table, creating a relationship between the two tables.
This connection helps maintain referential integrity.
Candidate key: Minimal set of attributes that can uniquely identify a record.
One candidate key is chosen as the primary key.
Other candidate keys are called alternate keys.
Composite key: Uses two or more columns together.
Because a student can enroll in many courses, and a course can have many students.
Normalization: Organizes tables to reduce unnecessary duplication and prevent insertion, update, and deletion anomalies.
First normal form: Requires each field to contain a single value rather than repeating a list.
Second normal form: Requires first normal form and removes partial dependencies on part of a composite candidate key.
Third normal form: Requires second normal form and removes transitive dependencies of non-key attributes.
For instance, instead of repeating a department name for every student, store departments in a separate department table and reference it using department ID.
This reduces duplicated data, and makes updates more consistent.
When related information is needed from separate tables, SQL joins can combine the matching rows.
Structured query language: Used to query and modify relational data.
The select statement retrieves rows, insert adds a record, update changes existing values, and delete removes records.
An inner join returns rows with matching values in both tables.
A left join returns every row from the left table, and includes matching information from the right table when available.
Joins commonly use primary key and foreign key relationships.
Transaction: Logical unit of database work.
Imagine transferring money between two bank accounts.
One operation subtracts money from the sender, and another adds it to the receiver.
If only one operation succeeds, the records become inconsistent.
A transaction groups these operations so they can be handled together.
Reliable transactions follow four important properties: Atomicity, consistency, isolation, and durability.
Atomicity: All operations in the transaction happen, or none of them do.
Consistency: Transaction preserves database rules and constraints.
Isolation: Controls how concurrent transactions affect one another.
Durability: After a transaction commits, its changes persist according to the database's recovery guarantees.
Commit confirms a transaction, while rollback cancels uncommitted changes.
A database stores organized information.
A database management system controls access to it.
Relational tables organize records.
Key: Connect related tables.
Normalization reduces redundancy, SQL queries and changes data.
Transactions protect reliable updates.
Keys establish relationships, joins retrieve related information, and transaction properties help.
